claim: Sensory dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons have a unique pseudo-unipolar morphology in which a stem axon bifurcates into a peripheral and a central axon.
source: Sensory dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons have a unique pseudo-unipolar morphology in which a stem axon bifurcates into a peripheral and a central axon, with different regenerative abilities.
evidence: This is a well-established anatomical description of DRG neurons, supported by scientific knowledge and cited in the manuscript.

claim: Peripheral DRG axons regenerate while central axons are unable to regrow.
source: Whereas peripheral DRG axons regenerate, central axons are unable to regrow.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about DRG axon regenerative capacity.

claim: Central axon regeneration can be elicited by a prior conditioning lesion to the peripheral axon.
source: Central axon regeneration can however be elicited by a prior conditioning lesion to the peripheral axon.
evidence: This is a well-known phenomenon in the field, supported by citations in the manuscript (Neumann and Woolf, 1999; Richardson and Verge, 1987).

claim: From early development, central DRG axons have a higher density of growing microtubules than peripheral axons.
source: Using this model, we observed that from early development, central DRG axons have a higher density of growing microtubules.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Microtubule polymerization asymmetry between central and peripheral DRG axons is present in vivo.
source: This asymmetry was also present in vivo and was abolished by a conditioning lesion that decreased microtubule polymerization of central DRG axons.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging of DRG explants shown in Figure 3.

claim: A conditioning lesion abolishes microtubule polymerization asymmetry by decreasing microtubule polymerization of central DRG axons.
source: This asymmetry was also present in vivo and was abolished by a conditioning lesion that decreased microtubule polymerization of central DRG axons.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: DRG axons have an axon-specific microtubule-associated protein (MAP) signature including spastin, katanin, CRMP5, and tau.
source: An axon-specific microtubule-associated protein (MAP) signature, including the severases spastin and katanin and the microtubule regulators CRMP5 and tau, was found and shown to adapt upon conditioning lesion.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The DRG MAP signature adapts upon conditioning lesion.
source: An axon-specific microtubule-associated protein (MAP) signature, including the severases spastin and katanin and the microtubule regulators CRMP5 and tau, was found and shown to adapt upon conditioning lesion.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J-M.

claim: Interfering with the DRG MAP signature in vitro abolishes central-peripheral asymmetries in microtubule dynamics.
source: Supporting its significance, interfering with the DRG MAP signature either in vitro or in vivo readily abolished central-peripheral asymmetries in microtubule dynamics and regenerative ability.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Interfering with the DRG MAP signature in vivo abolishes central-peripheral asymmetries in regenerative ability.
source: Supporting its significance, interfering with the DRG MAP signature either in vitro or in vivo readily abolished central-peripheral asymmetries in microtubule dynamics and regenerative ability.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G-K.

claim: Peripheral DRG axons show larger diameters than central axons.
source: In this respect, peripheral DRG axons show larger diameters (Suh et al., 1984), higher axonal transport rates (Komiya and Kurokawa, 1978; Wujek and Lasek, 1983), and increased regenerative capacity (Komiya, 1981; Wujek and Lasek, 1983) when compared to central ones (reviewed in Nascimento et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Suh et al., 1984).

claim: Peripheral DRG axons have higher axonal transport rates than central axons.
source: In this respect, peripheral DRG axons show larger diameters (Suh et al., 1984), higher axonal transport rates (Komiya and Kurokawa, 1978; Wujek and Lasek, 1983), and increased regenerative capacity (Komiya, 1981; Wujek and Lasek, 1983) when compared to central ones (reviewed in Nascimento et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Komiya and Kurokawa, 1978; Wujek and Lasek, 1983).

claim: Peripheral DRG axons have increased regenerative capacity compared to central axons.
source: In this respect, peripheral DRG axons show larger diameters (Suh et al., 1984), higher axonal transport rates (Komiya and Kurokawa, 1978; Wujek and Lasek, 1983), and increased regenerative capacity (Komiya, 1981; Wujek and Lasek, 1983) when compared to central ones (reviewed in Nascimento et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Komiya, 1981; Wujek and Lasek, 1983).

claim: DRG peripheral axons regrow following injury in vivo.
source: Interestingly, while DRG peripheral axons regrow following injury in vivo, the central axon only regenerates if a priming conditioning lesion to the peripheral axon is made (Neumann and Woolf, 1999; Richardson and Verge, 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Neumann and Woolf, 1999; Richardson and Verge, 1987).

claim: The central DRG axon only regenerates if a priming conditioning lesion to the peripheral axon is made.
source: Interestingly, while DRG peripheral axons regrow following injury in vivo, the central axon only regenerates if a priming conditioning lesion to the peripheral axon is made (Neumann and Woolf, 1999; Richardson and Verge, 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Neumann and Woolf, 1999; Richardson and Verge, 1987).

claim: A conditioning peripheral lesion induces molecular changes in DRG neurons enabling their central axons to acquire growth competence.
source: This conditioning peripheral lesion induces molecular changes in DRG neurons enabling their central axons to acquire growth competence, even in an inhibitory environment (Hoffman, 2010; Mar et al., 2014a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Hoffman, 2010; Mar et al., 2014a).

claim: Injury to the DRG peripheral axon induces a global increase in axonal transport that extends to the central axon.
source: We have previously shown that injury to the DRG peripheral axon induces a global increase in axonal transport that extends to the central axon, supporting axon regeneration (Mar et al., 2014b).
evidence: This statement refers to previous work by the authors (Mar et al., 2014b).

claim: At DIV21, cultured DRG neurons exhibit 4 ± 1% multipolar, 35 ± 8% bipolar, 17 ± 5% bell-shaped, and 43 ± 3% pseudo-unipolar morphologies.
source: At DIV21, we observed 4 ± 1% multipolar (with more than two neurites), 35 ± 8% bipolar, 17 ± 5% bell-shaped, and 43 ± 3% pseudo-unipolar DRG neurons (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: During pseudo-unipolarization, a reduction in stem axon diameter occurs.
source: While DRG neurons undergo pseudo-unipolarization (Figure 1D, Figure 1—video 2), a reduction in diameter (Figure 1D–E) coupled with an increased length of the stem axon (Figure 1D and F) occurs, mirroring in vivo development (Matsuda et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: During pseudo-unipolarization, an increase in stem axon length occurs.
source: While DRG neurons undergo pseudo-unipolarization (Figure 1D, Figure 1—video 2), a reduction in diameter (Figure 1D–E) coupled with an increased length of the stem axon (Figure 1D and F) occurs, mirroring in vivo development (Matsuda et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and F.

claim: Cell body bulging participates in stem axon formation.
source: This supports that cell body bulging participates in stem axon formation, as previously suggested (Matsuda et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D and G, supported by a citation to previous work (Matsuda et al., 2000).

claim: Pseudo-unipolar DRG neurons exhibit two axons with distinct diameters: a thin, central-like branch and a thicker, peripheral-like branch.
source: When measuring the two bifurcating axons 3–5 µm away from the DRG T-junction, we observed that pseudo-unipolar DRG neurons exhibit two axons with distinct diameters: a thin, central-like branch and a thicker, peripheral-like branch (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: Axonal diameter asymmetry is established early in DRG development, as bipolar neurons already displayed axons of different diameters.
source: This axonal diameter asymmetry is established early in DRG development, as bipolar neurons already displayed axons of different diameters (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The length of retraction following injury is the same for both peripheral-like and central-like DRG axons.
source: While the length of retraction following injury was the same for both DRG axons (Figure 2C), the duration of retraction was higher in central-like axons (Figure 2D), suggesting that these require more time to assemble a regenerative response (Koseki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The duration of retraction following injury is higher in central-like axons than peripheral-like axons.
source: While the length of retraction following injury was the same for both DRG axons (Figure 2C), the duration of retraction was higher in central-like axons (Figure 2D), suggesting that these require more time to assemble a regenerative response (Koseki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Over 50% of injured peripheral-like axons regenerate with an average length of 33.4 µm.
source: Moreover, whereas over 50% of the injured peripheral-like axons were able to regenerate with an average length of 33.4 µm, only approximately 10% of injured central ones showed the same ability, with a 3.8-fold decreased length (8.7 µm) (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Only approximately 10% of injured central-like axons regenerate with an average length of 8.7 µm.
source: Moreover, whereas over 50% of the injured peripheral-like axons were able to regenerate with an average length of 33.4 µm, only approximately 10% of injured central ones showed the same ability, with a 3.8-fold decreased length (8.7 µm) (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Peripheral-like axons have a higher flux of anterogradely moving mitochondria than central-like axons.
source: Aligning with in vivo data, in our in vitro model, peripheral-like axons had a higher flux of anterogradely moving mitochondria than central-like axons (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—video 1), further supporting the relevance of this system.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Both peripheral-like and central-like DRG axons have microtubule plus-end-out polarity.
source: Using the microtubule plus-tip end-binding protein 3 (EB3) to track growing microtubules plus-tips (Stepanova et al., 2003), we observed that while both DRG axons had microtubule plus-end-out polarity (Figure 3—video 2), the central-like axon had a greater density of growing microtubules (Figure 3C and D), and a slower microtubule growth rate (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—video 2.

claim: Central-like axons have a greater density of growing microtubules than peripheral-like axons.
source: Using the microtubule plus-tip end-binding protein 3 (EB3) to track growing microtubules plus-tips (Stepanova et al., 2003), we observed that while both DRG axons had microtubule plus-end-out polarity (Figure 3—video 2), the central-like axon had a greater density of growing microtubules (Figure 3C and D), and a slower microtubule growth rate (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Central-like axons have a slower microtubule growth rate than peripheral-like axons.
source: Using the microtubule plus-tip end-binding protein 3 (EB3) to track growing microtubules plus-tips (Stepanova et al., 2003), we observed that while both DRG axons had microtubule plus-end-out polarity (Figure 3—video 2), the central-like axon had a greater density of growing microtubules (Figure 3C and D), and a slower microtubule growth rate (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Microtubule polymerization asymmetry is established early in DRG development, as it is present in bipolar DRG neurons.
source: Notably, microtubule polymerization asymmetry was established early in DRG development, as it was already present in bipolar DRG neurons (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In vivo, 94% of microtubules in peripheral DRG axons and 95% in central DRG axons move with plus-end-out polarity.
source: In both central and peripheral DRG axons, most microtubules moved with plus-end-out polarity (94% and 95%, respectively) (Figure 3G, Figure 3—video 3), as observed in vitro (Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—video 3.

claim: In vivo, central DRG axons exhibit an increased density of growing microtubules compared to peripheral axons.
source: Also replicating our in vitro observations (Figure 3C), central DRG axons exhibited an increased density of growing microtubules (Figure 3H, naive), which was unrelated to differences in total microtubule density (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H (naive).

claim: The increased density of growing microtubules in central DRG axons is unrelated to differences in total microtubule density.
source: Also replicating our in vitro observations (Figure 3C), central DRG axons exhibited an increased density of growing microtubules (Figure 3H, naive), which was unrelated to differences in total microtubule density (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I and J.

claim: In vivo, microtubules in central DRG axons grow at slower growth rates than in peripheral axons.
source: Interestingly, and again replicating in vitro findings (Figure 3E), although having a higher density of growing microtubules, these grew at slower growth rates in central DRG axons (Figure 3K, naive).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3K (naive).

claim: A conditioning lesion decreases the density of growing microtubules in both peripheral and central DRG axons.
source: A conditioning lesion decreased the density of growing microtubules not only in the peripheral DRG axon but this effect extended to the central DRG axon (Figure 3H, conditioning lesion), abolishing central-peripheral asymmetry.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H (conditioning lesion).

claim: A conditioning lesion abolishes central-peripheral asymmetry in the density of growing microtubules.
source: A conditioning lesion decreased the density of growing microtubules not only in the peripheral DRG axon but this effect extended to the central DRG axon (Figure 3H, conditioning lesion), abolishing central-peripheral asymmetry.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H (conditioning lesion).

claim: The decrease in growing microtubule density after conditioning lesion is unrelated to differences in total microtubule density.
source: This was unrelated to differences in total microtubule density, as determined by electron microscopy (Figure 3M).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: A conditioning lesion increases the velocity of microtubule polymerization in both peripheral and central DRG axons.
source: In addition to decreasing the density of growing microtubules, a conditioning lesion increased the velocity of microtubule polymerization both in peripheral and central DRG axons (Figure 3K, conditioning lesion).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3K (conditioning lesion).

claim: Tubulin post-translational modification levels are identical in both DRG peripheral nerve and dorsal root.
source: Whereas tubulin PTM levels were identical in both DRG peripheral nerve and dorsal root (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), the microtubule severases spastin and katanin were markedly increased in DRG central axons (Figure 4B, C and, F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The microtubule severases spastin and katanin are markedly increased in DRG central axons.
source: Whereas tubulin PTM levels were identical in both DRG peripheral nerve and dorsal root (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), the microtubule severases spastin and katanin were markedly increased in DRG central axons (Figure 4B, C and, F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B, C, and F.

claim: DRG peripheral axons have increased levels of CRMP5 and tau compared to central axons.
source: Interestingly, DRG peripheral axons had increased levels of both microtubule regulators (Figure 4D–E and G–H), which by restricting severase access to microtubules may contribute to their decreased density of microtubule growing ends (Figure 3H, naive).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D-E and G-H.

claim: CRMP5 and tau restrict severase access to microtubules, contributing to decreased density of microtubule growing ends in peripheral axons.
source: Interestingly, DRG peripheral axons had increased levels of both microtubule regulators (Figure 4D–E and G–H), which by restricting severase access to microtubules may contribute to their decreased density of microtubule growing ends (Figure 3H, naive).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and known functions of CRMP5 and tau.

claim: Upon conditioning lesion, the uneven distribution of spastin, katanin, and CRMP5 in naive DRG is lost.
source: Interestingly, upon conditioning lesion, the uneven distribution of spastin, katanin, and CRMP5 in naive DRG (Figure 4B–D) was lost (Figure 4J–L).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J-L.

claim: The persistent asymmetry in tau distribution after conditioning lesion suggests that tau is specifically related to the establishment of structural differences between peripheral and central DRG axons.
source: Importantly, the persistent asymmetry in tau distribution (Figure 4E and M) suggests that this MAP might be specifically related to the establishment of the structural differences between peripheral and central DRG axons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4E and M.

claim: The density of Spastin and Dpysl5 transcripts in DRG axons is similar.
source: However, as the density of Spastin and Dpysl5 (CRMP5 mouse gene) transcripts in DRG axons was similar (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C), differential mRNA transport and local translation probably do not account for asymmetric distribution of these proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Differential mRNA transport and local translation probably do not account for asymmetric distribution of spastin and CRMP5.
source: However, as the density of Spastin and Dpysl5 (CRMP5 mouse gene) transcripts in DRG axons was similar (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C), differential mRNA transport and local translation probably do not account for asymmetric distribution of these proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: In peripheral-like axons, similar numbers of EB3 comets stop or cross past the bifurcation point.
source: In peripheral-like axons, similar numbers of EB3 comets stopped or crossed past the bifurcation point (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2G.

claim: In DRG central-like axons, a ratio of 3:1 microtubules polymerize beyond the bifurcation point, supporting a higher microtubule continuum from the stem to the central-like axon.
source: Conversely, in DRG central-like axons, a ratio of 3:1 microtubules polymerized beyond the bifurcation point, supporting a higher microtubule continuum from the stem to the central-like axon (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Δ2 tubulin is unevenly distributed between peripheral-like and central-like axons, being increased in central-like axons.
source: While the levels of polyglutamylated and acetylated tubulin (Figure 4—figure supplement 2H–K) were the same in the two DRG axon compartments, Δ2 tubulin was the single PTM that was unevenly distributed, being increased in central-like axons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2L–M).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2L-M.

claim: The absence of spastin abolishes axonal microtubule polymerization asymmetry in vitro.
source: In vitro, in wild-type and Spastin knockout (Brill et al., 2016) DRG neurons, the lack of spastin abolished axonal microtubule polymerization asymmetry (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The absence of spastin is sufficient to abolish the asymmetry of microtubule polymerization in DRG axons in vivo.
source: Live imaging of DRG explants from Spastin knockout × Thy1-EB3-eGFP mice showed that the absence of this enzyme was sufficient to abolish the asymmetry of microtubule polymerization in DRG axons, both in terms of EB3 comet density (Figure 5C and D) and velocity (Figure 5E and F), while total microtubule density was preserved (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-F.

claim: In Spastin knockout mice, total microtubule density is preserved.
source: Live imaging of DRG explants from Spastin knockout × Thy1-EB3-eGFP mice showed that the absence of this enzyme was sufficient to abolish the asymmetry of microtubule polymerization in DRG axons, both in terms of EB3 comet density (Figure 5C and D) and velocity (Figure 5E and F), while total microtubule density was preserved (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In wild-type mice, conditioning lesion leads to a substantial increase in the number of regenerating DRG central axons.
source: In wild-type mice, conditioning lesion led to a substantial increase in the number of cholera toxin-positive regenerating DRG central axons (Figure 5I and K).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I and K.

claim: In Spastin knockout mice, the conditioning lesion effect severely reduces the number of central DRG axons able to grow in the inhibitory environment of the lesion site.
source: In contrast, in Spastin knockout mice, the conditioning lesion effect severely reduced the number of central DRG axons being able to grow in the inhibitory environment of the lesion site (Figure 5J and K).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J and K.

claim: Spastin knockout DRG neurons extend 3.3-fold less primary neurites than wild-type DRG neurons when grown on aggrecan.
source: Under these conditions, Spastin knockout DRG neurons extended 3.3-fold less primary neurites than wild-type DRG neurons (Figure 5L and M), replicating our in vivo findings.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5L and M.

claim: Loss of spastin in DRG neurons impairs axon growth under inhibitory conditions.
source: This indicates that loss of spastin in DRG neurons impairs axon growth under inhibitory conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 5L and M.

claim: Interfering with the DRG MAP signature disrupts the asymmetry in microtubule polymerization of DRG axons.
source: In summary, interfering with the DRG MAP signature disrupts the asymmetry in microtubule polymerization of DRG axons as well as their ability to mount the conditioning effect.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Interfering with the DRG MAP signature disrupts the ability of DRG axons to mount the conditioning effect.
source: In summary, interfering with the DRG MAP signature disrupts the asymmetry in microtubule polymerization of DRG axons as well as their ability to mount the conditioning effect.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Microtubule polarity governs asymmetric distribution of cargoes in multipolar neurons.
source: However, in contrast to multipolar neurons where microtubule polarity governs asymmetric distribution of cargoes (Tas et al., 2017), the mechanisms underlying differential axonal transport rates in DRG neurons are not understood.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work (Tas et al., 2017).

claim: The mechanisms underlying differential axonal transport rates in DRG neurons are not understood.
source: However, in contrast to multipolar neurons where microtubule polarity governs asymmetric distribution of cargoes (Tas et al., 2017), the mechanisms underlying differential axonal transport rates in DRG neurons are not understood.
evidence: This statement reflects the knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: CRMP5 and tau inhibit the action of spastin and katanin by blocking their access to the microtubule lattice.
source: Recently, the microtubule regulators CRMP5 (Ji et al., 2018; Jin et al., 2022) and tau (Kadavath et al., 2015; Panda et al., 1995; Siahaan et al., 2019; Tan et al., 2019) were shown to inhibit the action of spastin and katanin by blocking their access to the microtubule lattice.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Ji et al., 2018; Jin et al., 2022; Kadavath et al., 2015; Panda et al., 1995; Siahaan et al., 2019; Tan et al., 2019).

claim: CRMP5, similarly to CRMP2, may support microtubule polymerization, enhancing microtubule growth rates.
source: Of note, CRMP5, similarly to CRMP2 (Fukata et al., 2002; Hou, 2020), may further support microtubule polymerization, enhancing microtubule growth rates in DRG peripheral axons (Figure 3K, naive).
evidence: This is an inference based on known functions of CRMP2 (Fukata et al., 2002; Hou, 2020) and experimental data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Low doses of the microtubule-stabilizing drug taxol reduce the percentage of retraction bulbs after central axon injury.
source: In this compartment, low doses of the microtubule-stabilizing drug taxol reduce the percentage of retraction bulbs after central axon injury (Ertürk et al., 2007; Hellal et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Ertürk et al., 2007; Hellal et al., 2011).

claim: Taxol-stabilized microtubules enhance kinesin binding.
source: Microtubule stabilization is also crucial to sustain efficient axonal transport, with taxol-stabilized microtubules enhancing kinesin binding (Dunn et al., 2008; Kapitein et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Dunn et al., 2008; Kapitein et al., 2010).

claim: The reduction in growing microtubule density following a conditioning lesion may contribute to microtubule stabilization, supporting axonal transport and regeneration.
source: Likewise, the reduction in growing microtubule density following a conditioning lesion may contribute to microtubule stabilization, supporting axonal transport and regeneration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and known effects of microtubule stabilization.

claim: Katanin shares similar severing mechanisms with spastin.
source: Notably, katanin shares similar severing mechanisms with spastin (Roll-Mecak and Vale, 2008; Zehr et al., 2017) and is partially regulated in a comparable manner.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Roll-Mecak and Vale, 2008; Zehr et al., 2017).

claim: Both spastin and katanin undergo biphasic regulation through tubulin glutamylation.
source: Both proteins undergo biphasic regulation through tubulin glutamylation (Lacroix et al., 2010; Szczesna et al., 2022; Valenstein and Roll-Mecak, 2016) and their severing activity is inhibited by tau condensates (Siahaan et al., 2019; Tan et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Lacroix et al., 2010; Szczesna et al., 2022; Valenstein and Roll-Mecak, 2016).

claim: The severing activity of spastin and katanin is inhibited by tau condensates.
source: Both proteins undergo biphasic regulation through tubulin glutamylation (Lacroix et al., 2010; Szczesna et al., 2022; Valenstein and Roll-Mecak, 2016) and their severing activity is inhibited by tau condensates (Siahaan et al., 2019; Tan et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Siahaan et al., 2019; Tan et al., 2019).

claim: Katanin plays a role in axon outgrowth.
source: Moreover, katanin plays a role in axon outgrowth (Ahmad et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2014), with RhoA negatively modulating neurite outgrowth via regulation of spastin and katanin (Tan et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Ahmad et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2014).

claim: RhoA negatively modulates neurite outgrowth via regulation of spastin and katanin.
source: Moreover, katanin plays a role in axon outgrowth (Ahmad et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2014), with RhoA negatively modulating neurite outgrowth via regulation of spastin and katanin (Tan et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study (Tan et al., 2020).

claim: At early days in vitro (DIV 7-14), pseudo-unipolar DRG could be reverted to a bell-shaped bipolar morphology.
source: Interestingly, at early days in vitro (DIV 7–14), pseudo-unipolar DRG could be reverted to a bell-shaped bipolar morphology, while at later DIVs (DIV 14–21), this transition was never observed (Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—video 2.

claim: At later DIVs (DIV 14-21), pseudo-unipolar DRG neurons cannot be reverted to a bell-shaped bipolar morphology.
source: Interestingly, at early days in vitro (DIV 7–14), pseudo-unipolar DRG could be reverted to a bell-shaped bipolar morphology, while at later DIVs (DIV 14–21), this transition was never observed (Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—video 2.

claim: The in vitro model replicates in vivo asymmetries in axon diameter, regenerative capacity, axonal transport, and microtubule dynamics.
source: Here, we developed an in vitro model where DRG neurons pseudo-unipolarize and mirror in vivo asymmetries, comprising those found in axon diameter, regenerative capacity, axonal transport, and microtubule dynamics (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by experimental data shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: The in vitro model serves as a valuable resource to understand DRG neuron biology, mechanisms driving axon regeneration asymmetries, and DRG-related diseases.
source: This model serves as a valuable resource to understand DRG neuron biology (including stem axon formation and possible sorting at the DRG T-junction), mechanisms driving axon regeneration asymmetries, and DRG-related diseases.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the model, based on the experimental findings.

claim: Stem axon formation may be driven by cell body bulging rather than fusion of the two neurites.
source: Regarding DRG stem axon formation, our findings support that it may be driven by cell body bulging rather than fusion of the two neurites, aligning with previous studies (Matsuda et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 1D and G, supported by a citation to previous work (Matsuda et al., 2000).

claim: At the DRG T-junction, the anterograde transport of mitochondria is biased toward the DRG peripheral-like axon.
source: In chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, the accumulation of Δ2 tubulin in DRGs and peripheral nerves disrupts mitochondrial motility (Pero et al., 2021). Accordingly, at the DRG T-junction the anterograde transport of mitochondria is biased toward the DRG peripheral-like axon, where Δ2 tubulin levels are reduced.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing Δ2 tubulin distribution and mitochondrial flux, combined with knowledge from a cited study (Pero et al., 2021).

claim: Δ2 tubulin may interfere with binding of molecular motors, contributing to establish a cargo filtering mechanism at the DRG T-junction.
source: It is thus possible that Δ2 tubulin interferes with binding of molecular motors, contributing to establish a cargo filtering mechanism at the DRG T-junction.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental findings and known effects of Δ2 tubulin.

claim: Excessive microtubule stabilization may be detrimental to axon regeneration.
source: Similarly to the growth cone where a delicate balance between microtubule stabilization and dynamics is necessary, a balanced regulation of microtubule dynamics in the axon shaft may also be required, as excessive stabilization may be detrimental (Gornstein and Schwarz, 2017; Pero et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Gornstein and Schwarz, 2017; Pero et al., 2021).
